paras.text: Reading Speed & Decision Biases, Audio Lecture

This chapter has two halves that feel related but are not the same problem. The first half is about reading faster. The second half is about deciding faster. The research says something different about each one, and mixing them up is how people end up buying a speed reading course when what they actually needed was more practice recognizing patterns, or end up trusting a confident-sounding number when what they actually needed was a base rate.
Let's start with reading.
Idea one. The real research on speed reading, and the one sentence that settles most arguments about it.

The authoritative review here is Rayner, Schotter, Masson, Potter and Treiman, published in Psychological Science in the Public Interest, volume seventeen, in May of twenty sixteen. It is called So Much to Read, So Little Time, How Do We Read, and Can Speed Reading Help. This is a review article, meaning the authors read through the existing research on how people actually process text and summarized what it says, rather than running one new study. That makes it the right single source to lean on for what the field as a whole believes.

Here is the headline finding, in the lead author's own words, reported by the publisher. There is a trade off between speed and accuracy. Skilled adult readers already average somewhere around two hundred to four hundred words per minute. The review's judgment is that it is unlikely a reader can double or triple that pace and still understand the material as well. Lead author Elizabeth Schotter put the bottom line this way. There's no quick fix.
Sit with that phrase for a second, because it is doing a lot of work. Not slower progress. Not a smaller gain than advertised. No quick fix at all.
Idea two. Why removing eye movements does not solve anything.

A lot of speed reading apps work by flashing one word at a time at a fixed spot on the screen, a method called rapid serial visual presentation. The pitch is that your eyes waste time jumping around the page, so removing that jumping should speed you up. Here is the number that kills that pitch. Eye movements account for no more than ten percent of total reading time. The other ninety percent is spent recognizing words and building meaning out of them, which an app flashing words faster cannot fix, because that is not where the time is going.

There is a second cost too. Normal eye movements let you jump back and reread a sentence that confused you. Flashing one word at a time removes that option entirely. And losing the ability to reread tends to hurt comprehension, not help it. So these apps are optimizing the ten percent that barely matters while removing a tool that actually helps with the ninety percent that does.
Idea three. The ceiling on extreme speed claims.

You will see ads and influencers claiming they read a thousand, fifteen hundred, sometimes two thousand words a minute with full comprehension. The review's own phrase for claims like this is that they are probably too good to be true. When researchers actually test people who look like exceptional speed readers, a pattern shows up. Those people usually already know a lot about the specific topic in front of them. Take away that prior knowledge and test them on something unfamiliar, and they remember very little and fail basic comprehension questions. So what looks like superhuman reading speed is usually two ordinary things stacked together. Strong background knowledge of the topic, plus skilled skimming. Neither one of those is a secret trick, and neither one transfers automatically to a brand new subject.
Idea four. Skimming is a real skill, just not the skill people think it is.

The review does not trash skimming. It treats it as legitimate for a specific goal. Skimming, meaning scanning for the most informative parts of a text instead of reading every word, works fine when what you need is the gist. It stops working the moment you need a complete, defensible understanding of every clause. Here is a question for you. You are handed a forty page homeowners policy and need to know fast whether it even mentions sewer backup coverage. Is skimming the right tool for that.
Pause and answer out loud.

Yes, skimming is exactly right for that first question, because you only need a yes or no on whether the topic appears at all. But if the answer is yes and you now need to decide whether to fight a denial under that exact clause, skimming stops being enough. Now you need the exact wording, the definitions section, and any endorsement that touches it, because a fast skim is built for gist, not for betting an argument on one sentence you might have glossed over.
Idea five. What actually makes someone a faster, better reader.

Not a technique. Practice. Reading broadly, building vocabulary, and getting familiar with how a given kind of document is structured. That last part matters more than it sounds like it should, and it is the bridge into the next idea, which is really the heart of why this whole track exists.

Idea six. Where real LSAT speed actually comes from. And I want to be very careful with this one, because everything I am about to say is a reasoned inference, not a cited finding. No study measured LSAT speed through pattern recognition directly. Label it that way in your own head every time you use it.

Here is the logic. Classic expertise research, most famously Chase and Simon's nineteen seventy three chess study, found something surprising about chess masters. Shown a real game position for a few seconds, they could reconstruct it almost perfectly. Shown a random, impossible arrangement of the same pieces, most of that advantage disappeared. Masters do not have bigger memories than novices. What they have is years of exposure that let them see a cluster of pieces as one familiar chunk instead of six separate items to track individually. That is called chunking.

Applied to the LSAT, as a derived inference, a well drilled test taker is not reading the stimulus paragraph faster than someone taking the test cold. They are recognizing the argument's shape almost instantly. A necessary condition flaw. A correlation dressed up as causation. An unrepresentative sample doing more work than it can support. They have seen that exact shape dozens of times in practice, so identifying it barely takes any conscious effort.

Here is the restoration parallel, since this is the example that will stick for you. An experienced estimator glances at a water stained ceiling and already has a rough scope in mind before he has measured anything. That is not because his eyes move faster than a new guy's. It is because the stain shape, the ceiling type, and the time since loss match hundreds of jobs he has already scoped, so the pattern gets recognized, not worked out from scratch. The gain on test day works the same way. It is not visual throughput. It is fewer seconds spent figuring out what kind of problem you are even looking at, because you already have a stored answer to that question.
Now we shift to the second half of this chapter. Deciding under uncertainty.
Idea seven. The classic source, and the three heuristics it names.

The paper to know here is Tversky and Kahneman, Judgment under Uncertainty, Heuristics and Biases, published in Science in September of nineteen seventy four. It names three heuristics. Representativeness. Availability. And anchoring. The paper's own framing is that these shortcuts are usually effective, but they lead to severe and systematic errors. Every bias I am about to walk through is one specific, named way that happens.
Idea eight. Anchoring.

A number you are exposed to first, even one you know is completely arbitrary, pulls your later estimate toward it. The paper's demonstration is almost comic in how simple it is. Subjects watched a wheel of fortune, rigged to land on either ten or sixty five, then estimated something totally unrelated, the percentage of African countries in the United Nations. The group that saw the wheel land on ten gave a median estimate of twenty five percent. The group that saw sixty five gave forty five percent. Same question, same unrelated wheel spin, wildly different answers. And here is the part that should bother you. Paying people for accuracy did not reduce the effect.

Claims example. A carrier opens negotiations at nine thousand dollars on a loss you scoped at twenty four thousand. You know nine thousand is lowball. Doesn't matter. Later compromise numbers, including the ones you propose, will drift closer to nine thousand than they would have if no number existed yet. The fix is not willpower, since the research shows willpower does not beat this. The fix is procedural. Get your own documented number on the table first, before theirs exists to anchor against.
Idea nine. Availability.

People judge how common something is by how easily examples come to mind, not by its actual frequency. The paper's own example. Seeing one car flipped over by the side of the road temporarily raises your gut sense of how common car accidents are, even though the real accident rate hasn't moved an inch. The paper also ran a word list study. Subjects judged a list to contain more men's names than women's names, or the reverse, purely based on which names were easier to recall, not on the list's actual makeup.

DFS example. One lineup with a hundred and fifty to one longshot wins a major tournament. That outcome is vivid, so it sticks in memory, and players start overrating how often extreme longshot builds actually cash. The real base rate hasn't changed. Only how available that one result is in memory has changed.
Idea ten. Confirmation bias.

The founding demonstration here is Peter Wason's nineteen sixty study. Subjects were shown the triple two, four, six, told it fit a hidden rule, and had to discover that rule by proposing their own triples and getting a yes or no answer each time. Most people guessed something like even numbers increasing by two, and then only tested triples that matched their own guess, collecting a string of satisfying yes answers. The actual rule was simply any ascending sequence. Of Wason's twenty nine subjects, only six reached the correct rule without a wrong guess first. Thirteen reached exactly one wrong conclusion. Nine reached two or more.

One naming note, because this is a real trap. Wason's study is the founding demonstration of this behavior. Whether Wason himself coined the specific two word phrase confirmation bias is disputed in secondary sources, so describe the study precisely rather than attaching that exact claim to his name.

Claims example. An adjuster has quietly decided a loss looks like wear and tear, then reviews the photos mainly hunting for evidence that fits that theory, while sliding past evidence of a sudden event. The review isn't neutral just because the adjuster believes it is. The fix, modeled on what Wason's more successful subjects did differently, is to write your theory down, then go hunting specifically for the one piece of evidence that would break it, before you go looking for support.
Idea eleven. Sunk cost.

Hal Arkes and Catherine Blumer defined this in nineteen eighty five as a greater tendency to continue an endeavor once money, effort, or time has already been invested, even when that past investment has no bearing on whether continuing is the right call now. Their demonstration involves a ski trip. Subjects were told they'd already spent a hundred dollars on a ticket to Michigan, then bought a better fifty dollar ticket to Wisconsin for the same weekend, and could only use one. Thirty three subjects said they'd go to the worse trip they'd already paid more for. Twenty eight chose the better, cheaper trip. A majority picked the worse weekend because of money that was already gone either way. Arkes and Blumer's own explanation for why people do this: nobody wants to appear wasteful.

Question for you. A general contractor has already spent six thousand dollars in staff time and legal letters fighting a carrier over a three thousand dollar disputed line item, and keeps escalating mainly because of what's already been spent. What should the decision actually be based on.
Pause and answer out loud.

The six thousand is gone either way. The decision should rest only on what it costs to finish the fight against what's actually left to win, exactly like the hundred dollar ski ticket should never have driven the trip choice.
Idea twelve. Base rate neglect.

This is ignoring the actual background frequency of something in favor of how well one specific case matches a stereotype. The nineteen seventy four paper's cleanest demonstration involves a description of a man named Dick. Subjects were told the personality sketch pool was seventy percent engineers and thirty percent lawyers, or the reverse, then read an uninformative description that matched neither stereotype. Dick is married, no children, high ability, well liked. Both groups rated his odds of being an engineer at fifty fifty, completely ignoring the base rate they had just been handed, because the description felt irrelevant to similarity judgment, so the explicitly stated numbers got dropped instead of used as a starting point.

DFS example. A running back posts a forty point outing off an unusual game script, and a player starts treating that one game as representative of his normal output. What's being ignored is the running back's actual season long per touch and target share rate, which predicts next week far better than one vivid, unrepresentative game.
Idea thirteen. Overconfidence, through what the paper calls the illusion of validity.

The paper's own definition: the unwarranted confidence which is produced by a good fit between the predicted outcome and the input information. Their flight training example makes this concrete. Instructors noticed that praise after a smooth landing was usually followed by a worse landing next time, and criticism after a rough landing was usually followed by an improvement. They concluded praise hurts performance and criticism helps it. Wrong. The real cause was regression toward the mean, a statistical pattern that has nothing to do with feedback at all. The instructors were confident in a causal story that happened to fit what they'd noticed, and confidence from a good fitting story is not the same thing as confidence earned by an actual track record.

Claims example. An estimator feels very confident in a scope because the damage pattern looks clean, one obvious water line, one obvious source. That tidy appearance is not itself evidence the number will hold up once demolition reveals hidden moisture or a second contributing cause. The fix is the same one that applies to every bias in this chapter. Check the judgment against its actual track record, not against how good the story feels while you're telling it.

Rapid recap. Reading speed has a real ceiling, confirmed by a twenty sixteen peer reviewed review, and claims of reading far faster with full comprehension do not hold up. Eye movements are not the bottleneck. Skimming is a real, limited tool for gist, not a substitute for a careful read of anything you'll rely on. LSAT speed, as a derived inference, comes from drilled pattern recognition, the same chunking mechanism that lets an experienced estimator read a ceiling fast, not from reading text faster. On the decision side, anchoring pulls your numbers toward whatever you saw first, even a number you know is arbitrary. Availability inflates the felt frequency of anything vivid or recent. Confirmation bias turns your own evidence search into a one sided hunt once you've already picked a conclusion. Sunk cost keeps you throwing good time and money after bad because you don't want to look wasteful. Base rate neglect lets one vivid case override numbers you were explicitly given. And overconfidence, the illusion of validity, mistakes a good looking story for a reliable prediction.
If any of the questions I asked gave you trouble, that's exactly where to go back and drill.
